title: The ‘reverse Kindleberger Trap’: reasons to worry about the next financial crisis
gist: Chatham House argues the next global financial crisis will hit a world in a ‘reverse Kindleberger Trap’: the incumbent hegemon (Washington) is unwilling to act as global lender of last resort, while the rising one (Beijing) is unable because the renminbi is still marginal. Because foreign holdings of US securities have swollen from ~$12tn to over $37tn and the real trade-weighted dollar is near a 30-year high, the next US crisis should produce capital outflow and a substantially weaker dollar — the mirror image of 2008.

themes.theme: Reverse Kindleberger: hegemon unwilling, challenger unable

insights.claim: Charles Kindleberger attributed the length and depth of the 1930s Depression to the failure of either Great Britain or the US to act as a responsible hegemon — an impoverished declining Britain unable to lead, and an isolationist rising US unwilling to.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The Kindleberger frame gives investors a checklist for systemic fragility — open trading system, policy coordination, lender of last resort — and all three are currently degrading.
insights.quote: the world lacked an open trading system, any credible coordination of economic policies, or a reliable international lender of last resort
insights.locator: A worrying feature of the next big

insights.claim: The modern version of the Kindleberger Trap is inverted: the binding risk is no longer the rising power's reluctance to stabilise the system but the incumbent power's — Washington's — unwillingness to do so.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Crisis playbooks that assume an automatic Fed/Treasury backstop for non-US institutions are mispriced; tail hedges on cross-border dollar funding deserve a higher premium.
insights.quote: Risk stems not so much from the unwillingness of the rising hegemon in Beijing to help stabilise the system; but rather from the unwillingness of the incumbent hegemon in Washington
insights.locator: These days, though, the new Kindleberger Trap

insights.claim: Kindleberger's core mechanism is that nationally rational protective actions aggregate into collective ruin — when each country protects its own private interest, the world public interest and ultimately all private interests are destroyed.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: In a fragmenting policy environment, assume coordination failure as the base case when stress-testing correlated drawdowns across regions.
insights.quote: When every country turned to protect its national private interest, the world public interest went down the drain, and with it the private interests of all
insights.locator: ‘When every country turned to protect

insights.claim: The overall configuration for the next crisis is one in which the dominant financial power is unwilling to manage it and the rising power is unable to, meaning neither leg of hegemonic stabilisation is available.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect longer, deeper drawdowns and slower normalisation than post-2008 analogues imply — duration of crisis, not just depth, is the variable to reprice.
insights.quote: the dominant power is the one that’s unwilling to play a responsible crisis-management role; and where the rising power is the one that is unable
insights.locator: All in all, then, the risk

themes.theme: The 2008 benchmark: scale of the Fed's global backstop

insights.claim: By the summer of 2010 the Federal Reserve had supplied $10 trillion at various maturities in response to the Lehman crisis, via collateralised lending facilities to global banks — especially European banks that had built large reliance on dollar funding.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: $10tn is the yardstick for what a credible backstop costs; any future response materially below it implies far wider funding spreads for non-US institutions.
insights.quote: By the summer of 2010, the Fed had supplied $10 trillion at various maturities.
insights.locator: The 2008 crisis

insights.claim: More than half of the Federal Reserve's crisis-era purchases of mortgage-backed securities were sold to it by foreign firms, making QE a direct transfer of support to the international financial system rather than a purely domestic operation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: QE's international incidence is under-appreciated: a future Fed constrained to domestic-only support removes a hidden bid for foreign-held dollar assets.
insights.quote: more than half the Fed’s purchases of mortgage-backed securities were sold to it by foreign firms
insights.locator: In addition, the Fed’s QE programme

insights.claim: Fourteen central banks had access to substantial amounts of dollar liquidity through the Federal Reserve's currency swap lines during the post-Lehman period.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Swap-line membership is the cleanest observable signal of who is inside the dollar safety net; watch which countries retain or lose access.
insights.quote: And fourteen central banks had access to substantial amounts of dollar liquidity from the Fed’s currency swap lines.
insights.locator: The 2008 crisis

insights.claim: The Fed's 2008-10 liquidity provision was self-interested rather than altruistic: without it, European banks and global asset managers would have been forced to dump their dollar portfolios at fire-sale prices.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Self-interest is a more durable predictor of future US action than commitment rhetoric — model backstops by asking whose losses land on US balance sheets.
insights.quote: If the Fed hadn’t provided this liquidity, European banks and global asset managers would have been forced to sell off their dollar portfolios at fire-sale prices.
insights.locator: Of course, the US acted in its own self-interest

insights.claim: Effective US crisis management in 2008 was rewarded with a safe-haven bid: foreigners bought nearly a trillion dollars of US Treasury securities in the 12 months after the Lehman crisis, and the dollar strengthened.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The reflexive 'crisis equals long dollar, long Treasuries' trade rests on a credibility premium that must be re-verified, not assumed.
insights.quote: foreigners bought nearly a trillion dollars of US Treasury securities in the 12 months after the Lehman crisis
insights.locator: And US credibility was rewarded

themes.theme: Transactional liquidity: swap lines as political favours

insights.claim: A US administration known for transactional behaviour is likely to be highly selective about which counterparties receive emergency dollar liquidity, breaking the presumption of rules-based access.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Country risk in a dollar crunch becomes a function of political alignment with Washington — price sovereign and bank funding spreads accordingly.
insights.quote: a Trump administration noted for its transactional behaviour could end up being highly selective about who it offers liquidity to
insights.locator: A Trump-era crisis

insights.claim: In October 2025 the US administration supplied a $20 billion swap facility to the Argentine central bank to stabilise the peso ahead of mid-term elections that threatened President Milei's authority — liquidity allocated on political rather than systemic grounds.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A concrete precedent that US dollar support now follows electoral timetables of allied governments — a tradeable pattern for EM sovereigns aligned with Washington.
insights.quote: the US administration supplied a $20 billion swap facility to the Argentine central bank, in an effort to stabilise the peso in the run up to mid-term elections
insights.locator: We’ve already seen this selectivity in action

insights.claim: A proposed US swap line for the central bank of the United Arab Emirates was discussed despite the UAE being flush with dollar liquidity, underlining that allocation is driven by alliance politics rather than need.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: When backstops go to the liquid and connected rather than the illiquid and systemic, the distribution of crisis losses shifts toward unaligned markets.
insights.quote: a bizarre possibility, less for the fact that the UAE is a key US ally, but more for the fact that it is a country rather flush with dollar liquidity
insights.locator: Earlier this year there was discussion

themes.theme: Politicised price discovery in the Treasury market

insights.claim: The market's growing ability to question the safe-haven status of US Treasury bonds is identified as a distinct structural problem for the next crisis, separate from fiscal arithmetic.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat the Treasury safe-haven bid as a variable, not a constant, when sizing crisis hedges; consider alternatives such as gold or non-dollar duration.
insights.quote: The market’s growing ability to question the safe-haven status of US treasury bonds.
insights.locator: Three problems stand out

insights.claim: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's support for the Japanese yen was designed to discourage Japan from selling any of the $1 trillion of US Treasury bonds it owns, instead directing Japan to pledge those bonds as collateral to borrow funds for its FX intervention.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Japan's $1tn Treasury stock is being actively managed as a political rather than market variable — a forced-seller scenario there is a live tail risk for long-end yields.
insights.quote: clearly aimed at discouraging Japan from selling any of the $1 trillion of US Treasury bonds that it owns, in effect directing Japan instead to use its bonds as collateral to borrow the money it needed to fund its intervention
insights.locator: The first was his effort to support

insights.claim: The announced increase in US Treasury buybacks of its own debt was motivated by fear that an unmanaged market would charge Washington interest rates on public debt at politically embarrassing levels.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Buyback announcements should be read as yield-suppression signals; they compress term premium artificially and set up a sharper repricing if the policy lapses.
insights.quote: motivated by fear that, left to its own devices, the market might charge Washington rates of interest on US public debt that could embarrass the administration
insights.locator: And Bessent’s more recent announcement

insights.claim: Repeated official interventions to manage the price of US government debt are inconsistent with the full price discovery that underpins a credible Treasury market.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Erosion of price discovery is a slow-burn credibility loss that shows up first in foreign demand at auctions and in the basis, before it shows up in headline yields.
insights.quote: Interventions like these are not at all consistent with the full price discovery that should be the hallmark of a credible US Treasury market.

themes.theme: Elevated dollar and the outflow asymmetry

insights.claim: The stock of foreign-owned US securities has risen from around $12 trillion to over $37 trillion over the past 15 years, driven by both good reasons (global technology leadership) and bad ones (absurdly high budget deficits).
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A $37tn foreign-held stock is the fuel for any outflow shock — the size of the position, not the flow, determines how violent a reversal can be.
insights.quote: the stock of foreign-owned US securities has risen from around $12 trillion to over $37 trillion
insights.locator: Elevated dollar

insights.claim: In inflation-adjusted, trade-weighted terms the dollar is nearly as expensive as it has been at any point in the last 30 years, leaving asymmetric downside from a starting valuation extreme.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Valuation plus positioning both point one way: long non-dollar FX and unhedged foreign holdings of US assets carry an embedded currency risk that is now skewed.
insights.quote: the dollar is, in inflation-adjusted, trade-weighted terms, nearly as expensive as it has been at any time in the last 30 years
insights.locator: As a result of all these capital inflows

insights.claim: The next US financial crisis is very likely to be accompanied by capital outflow rather than inflow, causing the dollar to weaken substantially against other currencies — the opposite of the post-2008 aftermath when the dollar strengthened.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The core tradeable call: a crisis-time short-dollar rather than long-dollar reflex, and FX hedges on US asset exposure that pay off in the same scenario as equity drawdowns.
insights.quote: a US crisis is very likely to be associated with a capital outflow, rather than a capital inflow, with the result that the dollar could weaken substantially against other currencies
insights.locator: What all this means is that

insights.claim: President Trump has repeatedly expressed a preference for a weaker exchange rate, arguing in July 2025 that a strong dollar prevents US firms from selling tractors, trucks or anything else — meaning a crisis-driven dollar slide may be welcomed rather than resisted by Washington.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not expect official dollar support in a sell-off; the policy reaction function has been inverted relative to prior crises.
insights.quote: a strong dollar means ‘you can’t sell tractors, you can’t sell trucks, you can’t sell anything.’
insights.locator: That might suit President Trump

insights.claim: There is a historical template for a hegemon prioritising a cheap currency over global stability: Great Britain created the Exchange Equalisation Account in 1932 to keep sterling cheap after leaving the gold standard in September 1931.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The 1932 analogue suggests an institutional mechanism could be built to entrench a weak dollar — watch for any US body or facility with an FX-management mandate.
insights.quote: Just as Great Britain created the Exchange Equalisation Account in 1932 to keep sterling cheap after it left the gold standard the previous September
insights.locator: Just as Great Britain created the Exchange

insights.claim: Beijing's global governance proposals published in June indicate a growing willingness to shape the international order, a shift from earlier reticence.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Chinese institution-building is the leading indicator for a parallel financial architecture; track which countries sign on before capacity actually arrives.
insights.quote: Beijing’s latest proposals for global governance, published in June, do indicate a growing willingness to shape international order.
insights.locator: China rising

insights.claim: China cannot act as a financial stabiliser regardless of intent because the renminbi remains a relatively insignificant currency in the international monetary system.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: There is no substitute lender of last resort in this cycle — renminbi internationalisation metrics are the gating variable for any de-dollarisation thesis.
insights.quote: China may be willing but remains unable to act as a financial stabiliser: the renminbi remains a relatively insignificant currency in the international monetary system.
insights.locator: China rising
